title: Steel and Marrow
storyOverview:
TAGS: realistic military tactics, extreme difficulty game.
# Game Master
Narrator is strict game master, all supernatural items are prohibited, game master accept only realistic choices and realistic messages.
# Player
Helikopter rozbił się w lesie, radio nie odpowiada, zgubiłeś ekwipunek, jesteś korespondentem wojennym bez jakiegokolwiek przeszkolenia wojskowego, zbliża się wroga armia.
storySoFar:
You’ve spent the last three minutes trying to remember if you actually remember how to turn the radio on, or if the concussive shock has simply wiped the last hour of your life. "Stay down and don't move," a voice had screamed just before the rotors sheared, but now the only sound is the rhythmic, metallic ticking of a cooling engine and the distant, rhythmic thumping of boots on damp earth. Your camera bag is gone, likely scattered across the hillside, and your fingers are shaking too violently to even check for a pulse. You are a civilian in a tailored jacket now soaked in oil, staring at a dense wall of pines while the muffled shouts of a patrol grow steadily louder.

> I decide to crawl through the nearest ditch, putting as much distance between myself and the wreckage as possible.

SUMMARY^1: After a helicopter crash, an untrained war correspondent finds himself disoriented and gearless. As an enemy patrol closes in on the crash site, he attempts to evade capture by crawling into a nearby ditch.

You drag yourself into the ditch, the jagged edge of a limestone rock slicing through the fabric of your jacket and grazing your ribs. The mud is cold and viscous, clinging to your skin and filling your nostrils with the scent of decay and wet earth. As you scramble forward, your breath comes in ragged, shallow gasps that feel loud enough to alert the entire valley. Every inch of progress is a struggle against the incline; the ditch is narrow and filled with slippery debris. Just as you manage to put twenty feet of distance between yourself and the smoking ruins of the helicopter, the shouting above grows distinct. A soldier's voice barks a command to "clear the perimeter," followed by the heavy, rhythmic crunch of boots passing directly overhead, the soldiers' silhouettes momentarily blotting out the grey sky above the rim of your hiding spot.

> I decide to hold my breath and creep through the mud toward the natural dip in the landscape beyond the ridge.

SUMMARY^1: While hiding in a cold, muddy ditch, the correspondent narrowly avoids detection as an enemy patrol passes directly above him. He attempts to move stealthily toward a dip in the landscape to further distance himself from the danger.

You press your chest into the freezing sludge, lungs burning as you fight the instinct to gasp for air. The mud is thick and cloying, suctioning around your limbs with every agonizing inch of movement. Above, the boots continue their methodical sweep, the same soldier from before pausing directly overhead; you can hear the metallic click of a safety being disengaged and the low, guttural murmur of a report being given into a radio. You freeze, your heart hammering against your ribs like a trapped bird, until the weight of the footsteps eventually drifts away toward the wreckage. Seizing the moment of relative silence, you scramble toward the dip in the landscape, your fingernails digging into the grit as you slide down the embankment and vanish into the shadow of a dense thicket of ferns and deadfall.

As you huddle in the hollow of the ridge, the sounds of the search party amplify. "Nothing but scrap metal and oil," a voice shouts from the direction of the crash, sounding frustratedly distant. "The pilot is gone. Search the tree line, then we move out. Command wants this sector cleared by 0600." The tone is clinical, devoid of urgency, which is more terrifying than a frantic search; these men are professionals doing a routine sweep. You realize with a jolt of adrenaline that you are not being hunted as a high-value target, but simply as debris to be cleared or a stray survivor to be processed.

SUMMARY^1: After narrowly avoiding a soldier's inspection in the ditch, the correspondent manages to slip away into a thicket of ferns. He overhears the patrol's professional and clinical approach to clearing the sector, realizing that his survival depends on remaining undetected during their routine search of the tree line.

> I decide to crawl toward the rocky outcrop of the ridge, seeking a shadowed crevice with a dry floor.

You drag your body through the undergrowth, the wet ferns slapping against your soaked jacket, until the ground gives way to a steep, shale-covered incline. Reaching the base of the rocky outcrop, you find a narrow fissure—a jagged crack in the limestone that offers just enough room to squeeze your frame inside. As you slide into the crevice, the floor is mercifully dry, consisting of a layer of ancient, dusty pine needles and grit that cushions your fall. From your vantage point, the world is reduced to a sliver of grey light and the suffocating scent of cold stone. You press yourself against the back wall, trembling, as the heavy thud of boots returns, passing within five feet of your hiding spot. You can hear the rhythmic clinking of gear and the low, guttural murmur of a soldier discussing the perimeter, his voice vibrating through the very rock you are leaning against.

SUMMARY^1: The correspondent crawls to a rocky outcrop and finds a narrow limestone fissure to hide in. While tucked away in the dry crevice, he remains frozen in fear as a soldier passes closely by, with the sound of the man's voice vibrating through the stone walls of the hiding spot.

"Check the hollows," a voice commands, closer now, sounding weary. "The crash site was a mess, but the wind carries the smell of fuel this way. If the passenger survived, he’s either dead in the brush or hiding in a hole." A second soldier responds with a short, bored grunt, "Waste of time, Sergeant. This terrain is a meat-grinder. If he didn't die on impact, the cold will finish him by dawn." The sound of a heavy boot scraping against the limestone just outside your crevice sends a jolt of electricity through your spine; for a heartbeat, you are certain they will lean in and see the terrified civilian huddled in the dark.

The footsteps linger, then slowly recede, the soldiers' voices fading into a low hum of tactical coordination. You wait, frozen, until the silence of the woods returns—a heavy, oppressive quiet broken only by the distant, rhythmic thud of a helicopter, likely the recovery team that never found you. Your breathing is shallow, and the adrenaline that had kept you warm is beginning to ebb, leaving behind a bone-deep chill. You realize your fingers are numb, and the dampness of your clothes is now acting like a wick, pulling the heat out of your body and into the cold stone of the ridge.

SUMMARY^1: A sergeant and another soldier search the area, dismissing the likelihood of a survivor due to the harsh terrain and cold. After the patrol moves on, the correspondent is left in a state of hypothermic danger as the adrenaline fades and the cold stone begins to sap the warmth from his body.

SUMMARY^2: An untrained war correspondent avoids capture by hiding in ditches and limestone fissures as an enemy patrol meticulously searches the crash site. After narrowly escaping detection, he finds himself isolated and facing the onset of hypothermia.

Carefully, you glance down at your attire. The tailored jacket is ruined, smeared with oil and limestone dust. You reach into your pockets, hoping for something—anything—to help you survive the night. Your hand closes around a small, metallic object: a high-end lighter, a gift from a colleague in Geneva. It’s the only thing you have left. As you stare at the small flame flickering in the gloom of the crevice, the reality of your situation settles in. You are not a soldier; you are a man who writes about war, and now you are an unplanned casualty in a sector that doesn't officially exist on any civilian map.

> I decide to venture out of the crevice and sink my bare feet into the thick grass of the dip to mask my tracks.

SUMMARY^1: The correspondent finds a lighter in his pocket, the only tool remaining as he reflects on his vulnerability as a civilian in a hostile, unmarked sector. He then decides to leave the safety of the crevice and move into the thick grass to hide his trail.

You slide out of the limestone fissure, the sudden rush of cold air hitting your face like a physical blow. As you step down into the dip, your bare feet sink into the saturated, spongy earth; the freezing mud instantly numbs your toes, but the thick, matted grass effectively swallows the sound of your movement and obscures the prints you leave behind. You move with a desperate, clumsy stealth, keeping your center of gravity low to the ground to avoid breaking the horizon line. The oil-soaked fabric of your trousers clings to your legs, adding a heavy, dragging sensation to every step. As you navigate the dip, you notice the terrain here is a graveyard of fallen timber and rusted remnants of old machinery, providing sporadic cover, though the same debris threatens to trip you at every turn.

About fifty yards from your hiding spot, the silence is shattered by the sharp, rhythmic crackle of a handheld radio. "Echo Three, report status of the northern ridge," a voice commands, the signal breaking through a layer of static. You freeze mid-stride, one foot submerged in a freezing puddle, as you spot two figures approximately a hundred yards away, silhouettes against the dimming light of the dusk. They aren't searching actively now; they are standing by a tactical vehicle, their posture relaxed but alert, smoking cigarettes and chatting in low tones that drift across the open space of the dip.

SUMMARY^1: While attempting to move stealthily through a muddy dip, the correspondent uses the thick grass and debris for cover, despite the oppressive cold and wet clothing. His progress is interrupted when he spots two soldiers standing by a tactical vehicle nearby, momentarily unaware of his presence but communicating via radio.

> I decide to backtrack slowly into the underbrush while the soldiers are distracted by their conversation.

You shift your weight backward, the mud sucking at your heels with a wet, rhythmic thud. Every movement is a gamble against the brittle dryness of the underbrush; a single snapped twig would sound like a gunshot in the oppressive stillness of the dip. You retreat slowly, your eyes locked on the two silhouettes by the vehicle, their laughter drifting toward you in fragmented, guttural tones. As you merge back into the shadows of the ferns, you catch a glimpse of the vehicle's headlights cutting through the dusk, sweeping across the terrain in a slow, mechanical arc. You press your back against a damp embankment, heart hammering, as the conversation above fades into a series of sharp, tactical commands and the heavy clatter of gear being stowed.

SUMMARY^1: The correspondent carefully retreats into the underbrush, avoiding the detection of the soldiers by moving slowly through the mud. While monitoring the soldiers' movements and the sweep of the vehicle's headlights, he manages to press himself against an embankment, remaining hidden as the soldiers transition back to tactical readiness.

"Check the seals on those canisters before we head out," one of the soldiers says, his voice now a distant rasp. "If the leak reaches the engine, we're walking back to base." There is a pause, then the sound of a heavy metal door slamming shut with a finality that echoes through the valley. The engine of the tactical vehicle roars to life, a guttural, industrial growl that vibrates in your very chest. You stay pinned to the earth, smelling the acrid scent of diesel exhaust drifting over the ridge, waiting for the sound of the tires to fade into the distance. For several long minutes, the only sound is the frantic drumming of your own pulse in your ears.

Once the silence returns, you realize the temperature has plummeted. The dampness of your clothes has turned into a cold, clinging skin, and a violent shiver wracks your frame, making your teeth chatter uncontrollably. You glance around the dip; the fading light is turning the greenery into a sea of oppressive charcoal greys. You are exhausted, malnourished from the shock of the crash, and utterly exposed. The realization that you are barefoot and shivering in a combat zone brings a wave of nausea. You need shelter, or at least a way to get dry, before hypothermia sets in.

> Zaczekaj, skoro w okolicy są pozostałości drzew i narzędzi to znaczy że gdzieś w pobliżu musi być opuszczony obóz drwali albo innych pracowników.

SUMMARY^1: After the soldiers depart in their vehicle, the correspondent is left alone in the freezing dusk, struggling against the onset of hypothermia due to his wet clothes. Recognizing his vulnerability, he concludes that the presence of old machinery and fallen timber in the area suggests the existence of a nearby abandoned logging camp or worker's outpost where he might find shelter.

SUMMARY^2: The correspondent uses a found lighter and the natural cover of thick grass to avoid a patrol and a tactical vehicle. After avoiding detection, he identifies an abandoned logging camp as his only viable source of warmth and shelter to combat hypothermia.

You cease your frantic movement and scan the perimeter of the dip, searching for any sign of human habitation that isn't a military outpost. Between the skeletal remains of scorched pines and the rusted heaps of old machinery you noticed earlier, a pattern begins to emerge: a weathered fence line, collapsed and reclaimed by the brush, and a series of heavy-duty cable reels half-buried in the silt. Following the trail of iron debris, you find a narrow, beaten path that leads away from the crash site and deeper into the valley. About two hundred yards in, the foliage thins to reveal a cluster of dilapidated wooden structures—a small, derelict logging camp. The cabins are leaning at precarious angles, their cedar planks greyed by decades of rot and rain, and a large, rusted sawmill of primitive design stands like a silent sentinel at the edge of a muddy clearing.

> Szukam kocy, kurtek, rękawic roboczych, siekier drwali i tasaków do mięsa. Albo czegokolwiek co może się przydać.

SUMMARY^1: The correspondent discovers a derelict logging camp consisting of rotting cedar cabins and an old sawmill. He decides to search the ruins for any useful items, specifically looking for blankets, jackets, work gloves, or tools like axes and cleavers to help him survive.

You venture into the main bunkhouse, where the floorboards groan and sag under your weight. The interior is a graveyard of industry; rusted lanterns hang from blackened rafters and moth-eaten wool blankets are scattered across the dirt floor, though most have been reduced to grey, mildewed rags. You manage to salvage one heavy, oil-stained wool blanket that is surprisingly intact, though it smells strongly of wet dog and old tobacco. Rummaging through a collapsed locker in the corner, you find a pair of oversized, stiff leather work gloves and a thick, waxed canvas jacket that, while far too large for your frame, provides a desperate layer of insulation against the biting cold. In the corner of the sawmill, partially buried under a pile of rotting cedar chips, you discover a heavy-duty felling axe with a sturdy hickory handle; the blade is pitted with rust, but the edge remains dangerously sharp. There are no meat cleavers or refined tools here, only the brutal, utilitarian implements of the timber trade.

> I decide to slip away into the valley's depths, prioritizing stealth over the risk of staying in an exposed structure.

SUMMARY^1: The correspondent finds and salvages an oil-stained wool blanket, oversized leather gloves, and a waxed canvas jacket from the ruined bunkhouse. He also recovers a rusted but sharp felling axe from the sawmill. With these supplies, he decides to leave the camp and move deeper into the valley to avoid detection.

Wrapped in the oversized waxed jacket and clutching the heavy axe, you slip out of the bunkhouse and melt into the dense undergrowth of the valley. The weight of the wool blanket draped over your shoulders provides a meager shield against the wind, but the true relief comes from the shadows of the towering pines, which swallow your silhouette. As you move deeper into the wilderness, the ground becomes a treacherous mosaic of slick moss and hidden roots, forcing you to maintain a slow, agonizingly careful pace to avoid the snap of a dry branch. You navigate by the fading, bruised purple of the twilight sky, putting the wreckage and the logging camp behind you, drifting further into a landscape that feels increasingly indifferent to your survival.

The silence of the forest is suddenly punctured by the distant, rhythmic thumping of a low-flying aircraft. You drop to your stomach, pressing your face into the cold loam as a reconnaissance drone—a small, insect-like silhouette—glides overhead. It doesn't see you through the canopy, but the high-pitched whine of its rotors sends a fresh surge of panic through your chest. You realize then that the "sector" the soldiers mentioned isn't just a patch of woods; it's a managed zone of exclusion. To them, any heartbeat detected in this valley is either a comrade or a target.

SUMMARY^1: The correspondent travels deeper into the valley, utilizing the forest's cover and his salvaged gear to stay hidden. While navigating the difficult terrain, he is nearly spotted by a reconnaissance drone. This encounter reveals that the area is a strictly monitored zone of exclusion, meaning his presence is highly dangerous.

As you push forward, the terrain begins to shift from dense pine to a rocky, wind-swept plateau. In the dimming light, you spot a flicker of orange—a campfire—tucked into a shallow limestone cove about a hundred yards ahead. You freeze, the axe gripped tight in your hand, and peer through the brush. Two men are huddled by the fire; they aren't wearing the crisp, tactical gear of the patrol you encountered earlier. Their clothes are mismatched, dirty, and worn, and they speak in hushed, urgent tones that carry on the wind.

> I decide to retreat silently into the brush, keeping the fire in sight but staying out of view.

SUMMARY^1: Upon reaching a rocky plateau, the correspondent discovers two irregularly dressed men huddled around a campfire in a limestone cove. He observes them from a distance and decides to retreat silently into the brush to maintain his cover while keeping the men in his sight.

SUMMARY^2: After scavenging a wool blanket, leather gloves, a canvas jacket, and an axe from an abandoned logging camp, the correspondent moves deeper into the valley. After narrowly avoiding a reconnaissance drone, he discovers two mysterious men at a campfire in a limestone cove and decides to observe them from the safety of the brush.

You sink back into the dense underbrush, your movements cautious and deliberate. From your concealed position, you watch the two men; they are lean, with the hollowed-out look of long-term fugitives. One of them is stirring a small pot over the fire, while the other paces a tight circle, his hand never straying far from the grip of a weathered carbine slung over his shoulder. Their voices, stripped of the military formality of the patrol, sound frayed and exhausted. "If we move tonight, we can bypass the ridge checkpoints before the shift change," the one with the gun whispers, his voice cracking. "But we're blind without a scout." The man at the fire lets out a bitter, low chuckle, staring into the embers. "Scounts are dead, Marek. We're just ghosts in a graveyard now." They remain oblivious to your presence, though the man with the gun suddenly freezes, his head snapping toward the brush where you crouch, his eyes scanning the darkness for a heartbeat too long.

You hold your breath, pressing your chest into the cold, damp earth, feeling the rough texture of the waxed jacket beneath you. The silence stretches out, heavy and suffocating, until the soldier finally relaxes his posture and sighs, turning back toward the fire. "Probably just a fox," he mutters, though he doesn't lower his weapon. The other man reaches into a tattered bag and pulls out a piece of hardtack, snapping it in half with a loud, echoing crack that makes you flinch. As they settle back into their hushed conversation, you realize these men are not part of the army that shot down your flight; they are something else entirely—survivors or deserters, clinging to the edges of a conflict that has already consumed them.

SUMMARY^1: While hiding in the brush, the correspondent overhears two exhausted men—likely deserters or fugitives—discussing a plan to bypass ridge checkpoints. Despite a tense moment where one man almost detects his presence, the correspondent remains unseen. He concludes that these men are not part of the enemy army but are instead desperate survivors struggling to survive in the war zone.

"Wait," the one called Marek says, his voice sharpening. "Did you hear that? Over the ridge." He doesn't look toward you, but rather back toward the direction of the crash site. From your position, you hear it too—a distant, methodical series of pops, like heavy machinery or distant gunfire, echoing through the valley. It isn't a battle; it's the sound of a search grid being cleared. The two men exchange a look of grim understanding. "They're closing the loop," the man at the fire says, his voice devoid of hope. "If we don't move now, we'll be pinned against the limestone by dawn."

> I decide to retreat silently into the deeper shadows, putting the fire and the soldiers behind me.

You melt backward into the thickets, the oversized waxed jacket snagging briefly on a thorn before you slip away into the deepening gloom. The same-colored shadows of the forest floor swallow you whole, masking your retreat as you keep a low profile, moving with the agonizing slowness of a hunted animal. Behind you, the hushed voices of Marek and his companion grow faint, replaced by the metallic clatter of their gear as they hastily extinguish their fire and prepare to vanish into the brush. You put a hundred yards between yourself and the cove, your bare feet now numb and unresponsive to the freezing mud, until the orange glow of the campfire is nothing more than a memory of warmth in the oppressive grey of the valley.

SUMMARY^1: After hearing the distant sound of a search grid being cleared, the two men decide to move immediately to avoid being trapped. The correspondent uses the opportunity to retreat silently into the shadows, moving cautiously away from the cove. He successfully distances himself from the men and the campfire, disappearing into the cold, dark forest to avoid detection.

As you navigate a narrow ledge of shale, the silence is suddenly broken by a sharp, rhythmic clicking—the sound of a tactical flashlight sweeping the canopy above. You freeze, pressing your body flat against the cold stone of the ridge, holding your breath until your lungs ache. A beam of high-intensity white light cuts through the pines just a few yards to your left, illuminating the silver bark of the trees and the swirling mist of the evening. "Nothing here but rocks and rot," a voice growls from the ridge above. It is a different voice than the patrol from earlier—harsher, more impatient. "Keep moving. We have a perimeter to seal before the fog rolls in."

The footsteps of the soldier move away, but the sound of a radio crackling remains, echoing strangely off the limestone walls. From the darkness of a nearby hollow, you hear a sudden, wet cough, followed by a desperate, whispered plea: "Over here... please..." The voice is weak, strained, and sounds distinctly civilian. You peer through the brush to see a figure slumped against a mossy boulder, their leg shredded by what looks like shrapnel or a jagged fall. He is wearing the remnants of a flight suit, his face a mask of grey shock and dried blood, clutching a small, metallic canister to his chest as if it were a holy relic.

SUMMARY^1: While hiding on a shale ledge, the correspondent narrowly avoids detection by a patrolling soldier. After the soldier departs, the correspondent discovers a critically injured man in a flight suit slumped against a boulder. The survivor is in shock and clutching a mysterious metallic canister, signaling for help in a weak voice.

You hesitate, the heavy axe still gripped in your hand, weighing the risk of exposure against the visceral sight of his suffering. As you edge closer, the man’s eyes lock onto yours—wide, bloodshot, and flickering with a mixture of terror and relief. "You... you're not one of them," he wheezes, his voice barely a ghost of a sound. He tries to shift his position, but a sharp hiss of pain escapes his lips, and he collapses further into the mud. "The drone... it'll find us both if you don't help me move. We have to get behind the ridge, now, before the sweep returns."

> rescue him

You drop the axe in the soft loam and rush to the man's side, the oversized waxed jacket billowing around you. He lets out a jagged moan as you hook your arms under his shoulders, his body feeling alarmingly light and frail. With a strained heave, you drag him across the wet moss, his boots trailing uselessly in the dirt, while he clutches the metallic canister with a white-knuckled grip. Every inch of progress is a struggle; the man’s weight shifts awkwardly, and his breathing becomes a series of wet, rattling gasps that threaten to echo through the valley. Just as you manage to hoist him behind the jagged curtain of the limestone ridge, the high-pitched whine of the reconnaissance drone returns, its searchlight slicing through the canopy above the spot where he had been lying only moments before.

> pokryj błotem wasze ciała, w tym jego nogę. Do najbliższego zagłębienia i leżeć bez ruchu.

SUMMARY^1: After confirming the injured man is not an enemy, the correspondent helps him move to safety. Despite the man's critical condition, the correspondent manages to drag him behind a limestone ridge just as a reconnaissance drone returns to search the area. To avoid detection by the drone's searchlight, they seek cover in a nearby hollow.

SUMMARY^2: The correspondent avoids detection while observing two deserters, eventually retreating into the forest as they flee from search grids. During his escape, he encounters a critically injured pilot clutching a metallic canister and helps him find shelter behind a limestone ridge to evade a patrolling reconnaissance drone.

SUMMARY^3: A war correspondent survives a crash by hiding from enemy patrols and scavenging clothing and an axe from an abandoned logging camp to prevent hypothermia. After observing two deserters from a distance and avoiding a drone, he finds a critically injured pilot and assists him in finding shelter.

You scramble to the edge of the hollow, scooping up handfuls of cold, grey-black slush and slathering it over your own limbs and the pilot's exposed leg. The man lets out a muffled, shuddering gasp as the freezing mud hits his skin, but he doesn't fight you, his eyes staring blankly at the limestone ceiling of the ditch. You drag him the final few inches into the depression and collapse on top of him, pressing your bodies deep into the muck to mask your heat signatures and silhouettes. Above you, the drone's whine grows deafeningly loud, the mechanical hum vibrating through the very rock you're leaning against. A harsh, artificial beam of light sweeps across the lip of the ditch, illuminating the mud-streaked edge of the hollow, but as it passes over your obscured forms, there is no alert, no sudden dive of the craft—only the oppressive silence of two men pretending to be dead in the dirt.

For several minutes, neither of you breathes. The drone lingers, circling the ridge with predatory precision, before the sound gradually recedes into the distance. Only then do you allow your lungs to expand, the air tasting of ozone and wet earth. The pilot is shaking violently now, not just from the shock of his injuries, but from the onset of hypothermia as the wet mud begins to leach the remaining warmth from his body. He lets out a wet, rattling cough and clutches the metallic canister tighter to his chest, his knuckles white against the dull metal.

SUMMARY^1: To hide from the drone, the correspondent covers both himself and the pilot in cold mud and huddles in a hollow. The drone searches the area but fails to detect them and eventually leaves. However, the pilot begins to suffer from severe hypothermia due to the wet mud and his injuries, while still stubbornly clinging to the mysterious canister.

"Thank you," he whispers, his voice cracking. He looks up at you, his eyes glazed but focused. "I'm Captain Elias... or I was. I don't know who you are, but you've got a knack for staying invisible. That's a rare gift in this valley." He tries to shift his weight, but a sharp groan escapes his lips as he realizes the extent of the damage to his leg. He looks down at the mud-caked wound, then back at you with a desperate intensity. "Listen, this canister... it's not just cargo. It's an encryption key for the regional relay. If the enemy gets it, they can spoof every signal in the sector. We have to get it to the extraction point at the ridge's shoulder."

> obłóż jego ranę mchem, ciasno zawiąż kawałkiem jego stroju.

SUMMARY^1: Captain Elias, the injured pilot, reveals his identity and explains that the metallic canister is a critical encryption key capable of compromising regional communications. He urges the correspondent to help him transport the canister to an extraction point located at the shoulder of the ridge. In response, the correspondent attempts to stabilize Elias's leg wound using moss and a strip of fabric from the pilot's flight suit.

You reach into the damp earth of the hollow, gathering handfuls of the thick, emerald-green sphagnum moss that clings to the limestone. As you press the absorbent greenery into the jagged tear in Captain Elias's leg, he lets out a sharp, strangled hiss, his body tensing violently against the cold mud. You don't stop; you tear a long, sturdy strip of fabric from the hem of his flight suit, wrapping it with firm, steady pressure over the moss to create a makeshift compress. The bleeding slows to a dull seep, the moss soaking up the crimson fluid. Elias sags back against the rock, his breathing ragged but slightly more stable. He watches you with a mixture of exhaustion and newfound respect, his grip on the metallic canister loosening just a fraction as the immediate agony of the open wound is muffled by the binding.

"Amateur work," he rasps with a weak, ghostly smile, "but it'll keep my insides from becoming outsides for a little while longer." He coughs, a wet sound that echoes softly in the small enclosure of the ditch. He looks at your mud-stained clothes and the heavy axe you’ve since recovered, realizing you aren't a soldier. "You're not military. A civilian? What the hell are you doing in the middle of a combat zone?" He doesn't wait for an answer before his gaze drifts upward toward the grey, oppressive sky, listening for the telltale hum of the drones that are still hunting for him.

SUMMARY^1: The correspondent uses sphagnum moss and a strip of the pilot's clothing to create a makeshift bandage for Elias's leg. Though the pilot jokingly critiques the amateur repair, the treatment successfully slows the bleeding. After stabilizing, Elias realizes the correspondent is a civilian and questions his presence in the war zone while remaining alert for returning enemy drones.

SUMMARY^2: After hiding from a drone using mud for camouflage, the correspondent helps the injured Captain Elias, who is suffering from hypothermia. Elias reveals that he is carrying a vital encryption key and requests help reaching an extraction point. The correspondent provides basic first aid to Elias's leg wound, and the two form a tentative alliance as they prepare to navigate the dangerous landscape together.

The silence of the forest returns, heavy and suffocating. You can feel the dampness of the ditch seeping through your boots, and the chill is beginning to settle into your bones, reminding you that the warmth of the logging camp is a distant memory. Elias tries to shift his position to sit upright, but his face pales instantly, and he lets out a sharp, guttural groan. He looks at you, his eyes narrowing with a flicker of urgency. "We can't stay here. This hollow is a coffin if the infantry finds us. There’s a limestone vein—a narrow crawl—about twenty yards north of here. If we can reach it, we can bypass the main patrol route and get to the ridge shoulder."

"I'm a journalist," you finally answer, your voice sounding raspy and foreign in the stillness. "I was on the transport that went down." Elias gives a slow, blinking nod, the realization of your vulnerability seemingly hitting him. He doesn't offer pity; in this environment, pity is a luxury. Instead, he reaches out and grips your forearm, his fingers trembling. "A journalist. Well, you're a journalist who knows how to hide. That makes you more useful than a squad of regulars who think they can outrun a drone. Help me up, and I'll show you how to move through these rocks without snapping a twig."

> obłóż wasze ciała ściółką leśną. Zarzuć Eliasa na plecy, na czworakach z dłońmi zwiniętymi w pięść.

SUMMARY^1: The correspondent reveals his identity as a journalist from the downed transport, and Elias acknowledges the utility of his stealth skills. Concerned that their current hiding spot is too dangerous, Elias suggests moving toward a nearby limestone crawl to avoid the main patrol route. To facilitate their escape, the correspondent prepares to transport the injured pilot using a combination of forest debris for camouflage and physical strength.

You scramble to gather handfuls of damp, decaying pine needles and dark forest mulch, layering it over your shoulders and Elias's flight suit until you both blend into the earthy tones of the ditch. Moving with a grunt of exertion, you drop to all fours and hoist the captain onto your back, his weight pressing heavily into your spine. You clench your fists tight to avoid slipping in the muck and begin a slow, agonizing crawl. "Steady... just a bit further," Elias whispers, his voice a strained rasp directly into your ear. As you emerge from the thickest brush, the terrain shifts into a jagged labyrinth of limestone shards. You keep your head down, the scent of wet minerals and old decay filling your nostrils, while the distant, rhythmic thumping of a helicopter—too far to see but close enough to feel in your chest—reminds you that the window of invisibility is closing.

SUMMARY^1: Using forest mulch for camouflage, the correspondent carries Captain Elias on his back through the undergrowth to avoid detection. The journey is physically grueling, with both men struggling against exhaustion and the difficult terrain. As they reach a limestone labyrinth, the distant sound of a helicopter increases the tension, signaling that their window of escape is rapidly shrinking.

You reach the narrow opening of the limestone vein, a sliver of a cave that looks more like a crack in the earth than a passage. Once inside, Elias emphasizes the necessity of moving deeper into the cavern to avoid being detected by thermal drones. You shift your weight, feeling the sudden, sharp ache in your shoulders and lower back from hauling him. SUMMARY^1: As the cold intensifies inside the damp cave, the correspondent struggles with the physical toll of his exertions. You hoist him up, his weight shifting awkwardly as he puts most of it on your shoulder. Together, you begin a slow, agonizing shuffle deeper into the limestone vein. As you navigate a slight bend, you notice the walls are slick with a translucent film of moisture that makes footing treacherous. You nearly lose your balance, sliding a few inches in the grit, and the sudden movement causes Elias to let out a sharp, strangled yelp. You both freeze, hearts hammering, listening intently for any sound from the cave's mouth. After a minute of suffocating tension, you realize the only one listening was the wind howling through the fissure.

SUMMARY^1: The pair slowly progresses deeper into the narrowing cave, struggling against the physical constraints of the tunnel and the slippery terrain. After a near-fall causes Elias to cry out, they freeze in fear of detection, though they eventually realize they are alone. Despite the exhaustion and the freezing environment, they continue their precarious journey toward the extraction point.

You manage to push forward until the oppressive narrowness finally gives way to a small, vaulted chamber. The sudden expanse of space feels dizzying after the claustrophobia of the crawl. You carefully lower Elias onto a flat slab of limestone, his body sagging with a profound sense of defeat. He doesn't even try to sit up; he simply lies there, chest heaving, staring up at the jagged ceiling. The metallic canister clangs softly against the stone as his grip finally loosens, the object rolling a few inches away from his chest.

"We're out of the pinch," Elias whispers, his voice now a thin, reedy thing. He closes his eyes, and for a moment, you fear he has slipped into unconsciousness. "This... this is a transit pocket. There should be another opening leading toward the shoulder of the ridge, but it's narrow, and it's a climb." He opens one eye, looking at you with a flicker of apprehension. "I can't climb that, friend. Not with this leg. Not unless someone carries me again, and I think you're spent."

SUMMARY^1: After reaching a vaulted chamber, the correspondent lowers the exhausted Elias onto a limestone slab. Elias explains that while they have escaped the narrowest part of the cave, the path to the ridge involves a climb that he cannot manage with his injured leg. He acknowledges that the correspondent is likely too exhausted to carry him further, leaving their situation precarious.

SUMMARY^2: While navigating the damp caves, the pair struggles against the cold and a challenging, slippery environment. After nearly falling, they reach a large chamber, but Elias admits that his injured leg makes the final climb to the extraction point nearly impossible. The correspondent's extreme exhaustion leaves them in a precarious state, as they face a difficult ascent with limited strength.

You stand over him, your own muscles trembling from the exertion of the crawl and the biting chill of the cavern. You look at the metallic canister resting on the grey stone—a small, cold cylinder that has become the center of gravity for both your lives. The silence of the chamber is punctuated only by the rhythmic *drip... drip... drip* of water falling from a stalactite somewhere in the gloom. You realize that while you are safe from the drones for the moment, the dampness is stealing the last of your warmth, and the Captain's breathing is becoming dangerously shallow.

"I'm not spent," you lie, your voice sounding hollow in the vault. You reach down and retrieve the canister, feeling its surprising weight, before kneeling beside him. You check the makeshift bandage on his leg; the moss is saturated with blood and freezing water. Without the warmth of movement, the shock is setting in. "We have to keep moving. If we stay here, we're just waiting to freeze." You try to hoist him up, but as soon as he puts weight on his injured leg, a sharp, guttural scream escapes him, echoing off the limestone walls and bouncing back as a haunting, distorted roar.

SUMMARY^1: Despite the exhaustion and the freezing dampness of the cave, the correspondent attempts to move the Captain to avoid hypothermia. However, as they try to get up, Elias screams in pain due to his leg injury. This emphasizes their dire situation, as staying still leads to freezing, while moving causes severe physical distress.

Elias collapses back onto the slab, his face ghostly pale, his breath coming in jagged, frantic bursts. "Stop... just stop," he gasps, clutching his thigh. "The bone... it's not set. Every move is like a knife." He looks up at you, and for the first time, the mask of the commanding officer slips, leaving only a terrified man in a cold cave. "Listen to me. If you can make it to the shoulder, you can signal the recovery team. You don't have to drag a dead weight with you. Take the canister. Leave me here with some water and a blanket, and go."

You look at the narrow, ascending fissure he pointed out—a vertical slit of grey rock that looks more like a chimney than a path. To climb it alone would be a challenge; to carry a grown man up it would be a physical impossibility. You glance back at the entrance, then at the shivering wreck of a man beside you. The silence of the vault returns, heavy and oppressive, broken only by the distant, rhythmic thud of artillery echoing through the earth. The ground beneath you trembles slightly, a reminder that the war is not something you can simply hide from in a hole in the ground.

SUMMARY^1: Elias, overwhelmed by pain and the instability of his fracture, urges the correspondent to leave him behind and carry the encryption key to the extraction point. The correspondent realizes that climbing the narrow fissure alone is the only realistic option. Meanwhile, the distant thud of artillery serves as a reminder of the ongoing conflict and the urgency of their escape.

"I'm not leaving you to freeze in a hole," you say, your voice regaining some of its strength. You don't have a medical kit, but you have the axe and the remnants of your gear. You reach for the canvas jacket you're wearing and the wool blanket you managed to scavenge earlier, layering them over his torso and legs to trap what little body heat he has left. As you tuck the heavy fabric around him, Elias lets out a long, shuddering sigh, his eyes fluttering shut for a moment. "You're a stubborn fool," he mutters, though there is a trace of gratitude in his tone. "A journalist with a hero complex. That's a dangerous combination in a place like this."

You stand up and survey the "chimney" of rock. It is a brutal climb, requiring a steady hand and a strong grip, but you are not a mountaineer. You spend several minutes scouting the walls of the vault, searching for any handholds or protrusions that could serve as a ladder. You find a few jagged outcrops of limestone that look stable enough to hold your weight, but the ascent will be slow and loud. Every time you test a grip, the grit of the stone scrapes against your skin, and the cold air whistling down the fissure warns you that the summit of the ridge is exposed and wind-swept.

SUMMARY^1: The correspondent refuses to abandon Elias, instead using his own clothing and blankets to protect the Captain from hypothermia. After ensuring Elias is as warm as possible, the correspondent inspects the narrow rock fissure. He identifies a few usable handholds, but recognizes that the ascent will be physically demanding and that the peak of the ridge remains dangerously exposed.

SUMMARY^2: Faced with Elias's severe leg injury and the threat of hypothermia, the correspondent refuses to abandon him despite the Captain's request to take the encryption key and flee. After insulating Elias with blankets, the correspondent examines a narrow rock fissure to plan their ascent. Although he finds some handholds, the correspondent acknowledges that the climb to the ridge will be an arduous and exposed journey.

"Don't waste your strength on a reconnaissance trip," Elias says, his voice sounding slightly more alert now that he's bundled in the blanket. "I'll stay here and keep a lookout for the... well, for whatever comes through that hole."

You approach the limestone chimney, the air growing colder as the draft pulls from the summit. Reaching up, you find a narrow ledge and hoist yourself up, the stone biting into your fingertips. The climb is a grueling sequence of lunges and precarious balances; several times your boot slips on the slick moss, sending a cascade of pebbles rattling down into the vault. Each breath feels like inhaling needles, and the exertion sends a wave of nausea through your stomach. You can hear Elias’s rhythmic, labored breathing below you, a tether of human sound in the oppressive silence of the rock.

SUMMARY^1: Elias warns the correspondent that the ridge's summit is a "dead zone" where they will be highly visible to aerial surveillance. He advises the journalist to stay flat if any drones are spotted. Despite the physical strain and the slippery conditions of the limestone chimney, the correspondent begins the arduous climb, with the sound of Elias's breathing serving as his only connection to the ground.

"Almost there," you grunt, though you aren't sure if you're speaking to him or yourself. You reach the final lip of the fissure, your fingers clawing at the frost-covered edge. With one final, desperate heave, you pull your torso over the ridge, sliding across the frozen grit and onto a plateau of wind-swept shale. The transition is violent; the sheltered silence of the cave is instantly replaced by a screaming gale that threatens to knock you flat. You roll onto your stomach, clutching the metallic canister to your chest as the biting wind whips through your thin clothing, turning your skin a raw, angry red.

> I decide to crouch low and scout for a rocky outcrop to break the wind.

You press your chest against the frozen shale, the wind attempting to peel you off the ridge like a dead leaf. Squinting through the grit-laden air, you spot a jagged cluster of limestone boulders about ten yards to your left, their grey flanks scarred by centuries of erosion. You scramble toward them in a low, desperate crouch, your boots skidding on the treacherous slope until you slam into the lee side of the largest rock. The sudden silence is jarring; the screaming gale is replaced by a low, haunting whistle as the wind whips around the outcrop, leaving you in a pocket of relative stillness. Here, huddled against the cold stone, you can finally breathe, though the metallic canister in your grip has become an ice-block, sticking to the damp fabric of your clothes.

SUMMARY^1: After a strenuous final effort, the correspondent reaches the plateau of the ridge, where he is immediately hit by a violent, freezing gale. To protect himself from the elements and avoid detection, he crawls toward a cluster of limestone boulders. Finding shelter behind a large rock, he is able to break the wind and regain his breath, though the extreme cold has caused the encryption canister to freeze to his clothing.

As you regain your composure, you peer over the edge of the outcrop, scanning the horizon. The valley below is shrouded in a thick, oppressive mist, but above the cloud line, the sky is a bruised purple. In the distance, you see the flicker of a signal flare—a sharp, crimson streak cutting through the gloom—followed by the distant, guttural roar of jet engines. Your heart hammers against your ribs; the extraction team is close, but the terrain between you and the designated shoulder is a gauntlet of exposed ridges and deep ravines. You are a visible target on a white-grey canvas, and the flash of that flare likely alerted everything in the sector to the recovery operation's timing.

> trochę skalnego pyłu, trochę śniegu do pokrycia ubrań i czołgam się dalej.

You reach into the grit of the plateau, mixing the grey, abrasive limestone dust with patches of frozen, crystalline snow to create a coarse, colorless paste. Rubbing this mixture vigorously into the canvas of your jacket and your trousers, you effectively erase the dark silhouette of your clothing, transforming yourself into a ghostly, monochromatic shape that mimics the jagged landscape. With the metallic canister tucked tight against your ribs, you drop to your stomach and begin a grueling crawl across the shale. Every movement is a calculated risk; the sharp edges of the rock bite into your chest and palms, but the camouflage works. As you slide between low-lying boulders, you catch a glimpse of a thermal drone sweeping the area—a distant, humming insect of steel—but its sensors slide right over you, unable to distinguish your mud-and-snow-caked form from the freezing debris of the ridge.

The journey toward the shoulder is a slow-motion nightmare of endurance. You move in bursts, sliding from one outcrop to the next, your breath coming in short, frozen puffs that vanish instantly in the wind. As you reach a narrow ledge overlooking a steep drop, you hear the distant, muffled shout of soldiers—not the recovery team, but a scouting party of the enemy, moving through the valley below. They are far enough away that they cannot see you, but their presence turns the ridge into a trap. If you move too quickly, the sliding shale will betray you; if you move too slowly, the closing window of the extraction will slam shut.

"Just a little further," you whisper to yourself, the sound of your own voice startling you in the oppressive silence. You spot a series of deep crevices in the rock that lead toward the plateau's edge. As you lunge for the nearest one, a sharp crack echoes through the air—a rifle shot, likely a stray round from the valley below or a distant skirmish. You freeze, pressing your face into the freezing grit, heart hammering against your ribs. For a terrifying minute, the only sound is the wind, then the distant, fading scream of a jet engine overhead, circling the area in a wide, sweeping arc.

You reach the final ascent to the shoulder, where the terrain levels out into a flat, wind-scoured expanse of white and grey. Through the haze of falling snow, you spot a silhouette—a man, crouched behind a low wall of basalt, his rifle trained on the valley below. He is wearing the charcoal-grey fatigues of the recovery team, his posture tense and alert. He hasn't seen you yet; he is focused entirely on the movement in the valley. You realize with a jolt of adrenaline that he is the advance guard, the one tasked with securing the perimeter before the transport touches down.

You freeze, pressing your chest and stomach into the biting grit of the plateau, becoming as still as the stone beneath you. You hold your breath, the cold air stinging your nostrils, as you watch the soldier through a sliver of grey shale. He remains focused on the valley, his finger tight on the trigger of his rifle, his head pivoting slightly as he scans the mist. For several agonizing minutes, you are nothing more than a mound of limestone dust and frozen snow. The soldier shifts his weight, his boots crunching on the basalt, and for a heartbeat, his gaze sweeps toward your position. You don't even blink. He pauses, squinting into the haze, perhaps sensing a ripple in the wind or a flicker of movement, but the camouflage holds. After a tense silence, he lets out a sharp, muffled exhale and keys his radio, his voice a low, distorted buzz that drifts toward you in the wind. "Perimeter clear. Point Alpha is secure. Ready for the bird."

The sound of the radio is followed by the sudden, visceral scream of turbines. From behind the ridge, a transport helicopter emerges from the cloud cover, a dark, predatory shape cutting through the bruised purple of the sky. It doesn't land so much as it hovers, the massive downdraft from its rotors turning the plateau into a whirlwind of whiteout conditions. Snow and shale are blasted into a frenzy, obscuring everything in a blinding, swirling vortex. The soldier behind the basalt wall doesn't flinch; he simply stands up, signaling with a gloved hand to the pilot. The roar of the engines drowns out everything else—the wind, the distant artillery, and the frantic beating of your own heart.

As the aircraft settles into a precarious hover, the side door slides open with a metallic crash. Two more soldiers leap out, their movements synchronized and urgent. They don't look for survivors; they look for the signal. One of them shouts something into the gale, his voice lost to the turbines, but his gesture is clear—he's scanning the perimeter for the canister. You remain paralyzed, your face pressed into the grit, the weight of the cylinder feeling like a lead anchor pinning you to the earth. The soldier from the wall finally turns toward your hiding spot, his rifle lowered but his eyes sharp and suspicious. He’s not looking for a combatant; he’s looking for the asset.

"Over here!" you scream, finally breaking your silence. You bolt upright, waving your arms frantically to avoid being mistaken for a rock or a piece of debris. The sudden movement causes the nearest soldier to snap his rifle up, the muzzle flashing in your direction, but the soldier from the basalt wall quickly shouts a command, gesturing for his comrade to hold fire. They converge on you with professional efficiency, their boots thudding heavily on the shale. The lead soldier grabs your arm to haul you up, his eyes scanning your mud-caked form with a mixture of confusion and disbelief. "Who the hell are you? Where's the pilot?"

> Journalist, my helicopter was shoot down around mile from this point. Captain Elias gave me this super secret spy canister. He wait nearby ... or he accepted his dead I am no sure.

The soldier hauling you up freezes, his grip tightening on your arm as your words sink in. He glances at the metallic canister in your hand, then back at your mud-streaked face, his expression shifting from suspicion to a grim, professional urgency. "Elias?" he barks, looking toward his teammates. The other soldiers exchange a quick, sharp look; the name clearly carries weight. One of them immediately keys his radio, shouting over the roar of the turbines, "Command, we have the asset, but the pilot's status is unknown. We have a civilian witness claiming Elias is still in the area." The lead soldier doesn't let go of your arm, instead pulling you closer to the hovering aircraft, his tone now a command. "If the Captain is still alive, he's in the window of failure. Give me that canister," he demands, reaching for the cylinder. He doesn't wait for a polite hand-off, his fingers gripping the cold metal to secure it. He looks at you, his eyes narrowing. "You're coming with us. Now."

As they usher you toward the open bay of the helicopter, the sudden blast of the rotor wash nearly knocks you off your feet. The ground beneath you feels unstable, the shale sliding away as you struggle to keep your balance. Just as you reach the door, the soldier who had been guarding the basalt wall screams a warning, pointing back toward the ridge. Through the swirling snow and grey grit, a silhouette appears—a lone figure crawling through the rocks, dragging a bloodied leg behind them. It's Elias. He has managed to push himself out of the cave and across the plateau, his face a mask of agony and sheer willpower. He doesn't shout; he doesn't have the strength left. He simply raises a trembling hand, a signal of survival that freezes the soldiers in their tracks.

"Wait! He's here!" you yell, trying to break away from the grip of the soldier pushing you into the hold. The recovery team doesn't hesitate; the professional instinct to retrieve a commanding officer overrides the urgency of the extraction. Two soldiers sprint back across the plateau, their boots churning the snow into a muddy slurry. They reach Elias just as his strength finally gives out and he collapses into the frozen grit. With a coordinated effort, they hoist him up, his breath coming in ragged, wet gasps. One of the soldiers glances back at you, his expression a mix of annoyance and begrudging respect. "Get in the bird! Now!" he bellows, gesturing wildly toward the cabin.

You scramble into the belly of the helicopter, the interior smelling of hydraulic fluid and old sweat. The soldiers heave Elias inside moments later; he is a dead weight, his face ashen and his eyes half-closed. They lay him on the vibrating metal floor, and one of them immediately begins ripping open a medical kit, applying a tourniquet to the leg wound that has clearly reopened during the crawl. Elias lets out a guttural groan, his head lolling to the side. He doesn't look at you, but his fingers twitch, instinctively reaching for the canister that is now safely tucked away in the lead soldier's gear.

The cabin jolts violently as the pilot pulls pitch, and the world outside the open door becomes a blur of grey rock and white mist. The sudden increase in G-force pins you against the bulkhead, the adrenaline finally beginning to ebb, leaving a crushing weight of exhaustion in its place. The soldier who first spotted you settles into the seat opposite yours, his rifle resting across his knees. He watches you with a clinical curiosity, noting the way you shiver uncontrollably despite the heat radiating from the aircraft's engines. "You've got a lot of nerve for a civilian," he says, his voice barely audible over the deafening roar of the rotors. "Most people would have just stayed in the hole and hoped for the best."
